messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: SSE2 + Eigen parallelize matrix ops
parts:
[move discussion to stan-dev]

On 5/21/13 6:24 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> Wow, I didn't realize that the Eigen benchmark results were that compelling.
>
> Three more questions:
> 1. Do we have the relevant optimization flags enabled to let Eigen
> take advantage of things like SSE?

Egads! It looks like it's not on by default. And we
haven't turned them on explicitly in the makefiles.

Any advice on how to configure g++ and clang++ to do
this in a cross-platform compatible way?

A quick scan indicates that for g++ and clang++ indicates
that we need something like

-march=native

to enable an architecture that supports SSE(2) and then
we need to explicitly set the SSE2 flag:

-msse2

Do we also need to set just SSE?

> 2. Are we letting Eigen parallelize matrix operations?

Not that I know of. This we should also check for config.
If we're running multiple chains in parallel, we probably don't
want to parallelize matrix ops. Otherwise, we probably do.

Is there a way we can turn it on at run time or is it a compile-time
option?

> 3. Do we have specialized adjoint computations for matrix ops yet? 1
> and 2 won't do much good until we do.

Yes, we have them for most ops and Marcus has been
continuing to add more.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: RStan vs. R's glm() function for logistic regression
parts:
[move to stan-dev]

If we can do optimization faster than R's builtins,
that's fantastic.

I was not counting data read times because I was
starting with the data in R and Jiqiang wrote a tight
integration there.

Of course, reading 30MB would be faster in a format other
than R dump. It's an intrinsically slow format and the code's
hardly optimized.

And yes, I have a nice new core i7 Macbook Pro which took
3s in R, with no data read time.

- Bob

On 5/21/13 6:50 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Ok, I just did a quick test of BFGS using the model and data generation scripts Bob sent. This is with K = 160 and N =
> 10,000
>
> Marcus-Brubakers-MacBook-Pro:stan mbrubake$ time ./logistic --data=logisitic.data --point_estimate_bfgs --init=0 --refresh=5
> STAN OPTIMIZATION COMMAND
> data = logisitic.data
> init = 0
> output = samples.csv
> save_warmup = 0
> epsilon = -1
> seed = 3496505751 (randomly generated)
> initial log joint probability = -6931.47
> Iter log prob ||dx|| ||grad|| alpha alpha0 # evals Notes
> 1 -1781.82 3.99246 514.407 0.001 0.001 2
> 5 -1148.86 1.55728 151.342 1 1 6
> 10 -1030.79 0.0556683 6.50517 1 1 11
> 15 -1030.66 0.00178793 0.189879 1 1 16
> 20 -1030.66 0.000108344 0.00874977 1 1 21
> 25 -1030.66 1.7213e-06 0.000248864 1 1 26
> 30 -1030.66 8.76987e-08 3.63224e-06 1 1 71
> 32 -1030.66 1.09407e-08 2.35202e-06 0.0001565 0.001 148 LS failed, BFGS reset;
> Optimization terminated with code -1
>
> real 0m13.129s
> user 0m12.912s
> sys 0m0.188s
>
> So, in short, 13s. Now, a few caveats:
>
> 1) The BFGS implementation is currently bad at detecting convergence. If it was better at this, that would probably be 10s.
> 2) Somewhere around 7 or 8 seconds is spent before the first iteration is ever run. I suspect that most of this is
> caused by reading in the data from the R dump format.
> 3) This timing is on a different machine than Bob's, but I suspect my 3-4yr old macbook pro is probably slower than
> whatever Bob was running on.
>
> If we assumed that 1&2 could be resolved, the time would be more like 3 or 4 seconds which is basically the same as the
> glm() reported on what is a presumably faster machine.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
